Plan by age · Stage 2 of 5

Ages 50–54: The catch-up years

At 50 the tax code lets you save more each year, and for many households the end of child-raising costs frees up cash at the same time. These are often the most powerful saving years of a career.

This is also when midlife changes tend to arrive: health costs that jump, a divorce, or the death of a spouse. Each one changes the plan, and each has specific rules worth knowing before you need them.

  2. 50–54The catch-up years

Birthdays that matter

  • 50Catch-up contributions to 401(k)s, 403(b)s, governmental 457s and IRAs begin in the calendar year you turn 50. IRS: Catch-up contributions
  • 55 (next)Separating from an employer in or after the year you turn 55 can open penalty-free access to that employer's plan. IRS: Exceptions to tax on early distributions

  1. Catch-up contributions start at 50

  4. Divorce or widowhood in midlife

Catch-up contributions start at 50

What's happening

You can add catch-up contributions in any year you are 50 or older by December 31. You do not need to be behind to use them. Starting in 2026, higher earners must make their workplace catch-ups as Roth contributions.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Roth or traditional for catch-ups when you have the choice.
  • Where extra savings go once the workplace plan and IRA are full: an HSA, then a taxable brokerage account.

Common mistakes

  • Waiting until 'later in your 50s'. Each year of catch-ups you skip is gone for good.
  • Missing the deadline: workplace catch-ups have to go through payroll by the end of the plan year.

Key numbers for 2026

  • $8,000Catch-up contribution (age 50+)2026, for most 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans and the TSP, for a total of $32,500.Source: IRS: 2026 401(k) and IRA limits (IR-2025-111)
  • $1,100IRA catch-up2026, on top of the $7,500 IRA limit.Source: IRS: 2026 401(k) and IRA limits (IR-2025-111)
  • $150,000Roth catch-up wage thresholdPrior-year Social Security wages from the plan sponsor above this mean catch-ups must be Roth (applies from 2026).Source: Federal Register: Catch-up contributions final rule (Sept. 2025)

Kids leaving home

What's happening

When the last child becomes independent, a large slice of spending can stop. That money becomes savings only if you redirect it on purpose. Adult children may still need help with health coverage, a first apartment or a car.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Helping adult children versus funding your own retirement.
  • Downsizing now, later, or never.

Common mistakes

  • Letting the freed-up cash disappear into everyday spending.
  • Co-signing a loan you could not afford to repay yourself.

Key numbers for 2026

  • up to age 26Health coverage for adult childrenChildren can stay on a parent's health plan until 26, even if married or not living at home.Source: HealthCare.gov: Coverage for young adults under 26

Health costs jump

What's happening

Premiums and out-of-pocket costs tend to rise with age, and employers are passing more of the increase to workers. The plan you pick each open enrollment, and how you use an HSA, now matters more.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • High-deductible plan plus HSA versus a traditional plan.
  • Spending the HSA now versus letting it grow for retirement health costs.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing the lowest premium without checking the deductible and the out-of-pocket maximum.
  • Leaving HSA money in cash for decades.

Key numbers for 2026

  • $4,400 / $8,750HSA contribution limit2026, self-only / family coverage.Source: IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-19: 2026 HSA limits
  • $8,500 / $17,000High-deductible plan out-of-pocket maximum2026, self-only / family, for HSA-eligible plans.Source: IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-19: 2026 HSA limits

Divorce or widowhood in midlife

What's happening

A divorce or a spouse's death changes income, taxes, benefits and every beneficiary form at once. Social Security has specific rules for divorced and surviving spouses that many people never hear about.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Keeping the house versus a larger share of retirement accounts.
  • When a surviving spouse should claim survivor versus own retirement benefits.

Common mistakes

  • Cashing out retirement money to settle a divorce instead of transferring it under the court order.
  • Forgetting that a divorced spouse may qualify for benefits on an ex-spouse's record if the marriage lasted 10 years.

Key numbers for 2026

  • 10-year marriageDivorced-spouse benefitsA divorced spouse can collect on an ex's record from 62 if the marriage lasted at least 10 years and they are unmarried.Source: SSA: Benefits for divorced spouses
  • from age 60Survivor benefitsA widow or widower can collect reduced survivor benefits from 60 (50 if disabled).Source: SSA: Social Security if your spouse passes away
  • QDROEarly-withdrawal tax exceptionPlan payments to an alternate payee under a qualified domestic relations order avoid the 10% additional tax.Source: IRS: Exceptions to tax on early distributions

What's coming next

Ages 55–59: Early-exit options

In the late 50s the rules on reaching your own money loosen: the rule of 55 for workplace plans, then 59½ for IRAs. That makes an earlier exit possible, sometimes by choice and sometimes because of a layoff or buyout.

  • Early access rules: 55 and 59½
  • Job loss, buyout or forced early retirement
  • Pension or lump sum choices
  • Downsizing or relocating, including abroad
